extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political philosophy and public policy (those interested in liberty, censorship, and the limits of social/governmental authority)
extracted.subtask_description: A normative framework for judging when society or government may legitimately interfere with an individual's actions, opinions, or associations; addresses liberty of thought, speech, personal conduct, and exceptions. The text articulates principles (notably the harm principle), relevant exceptions, and practical guidance for policymaking and social judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle (sole end of legitimate interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection — to prevent harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power may be rightfully exercised over a member of a civilized community, against his will, only to prevent harm to others. This is stated as the central governing principle for when compulsion and control are legitimate; it applies whether the means are legal penalties or moral coercion of public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own good not sufficient warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for compulsion by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons such as 'it will make him happier' or 'it would be wiser' are grounds for persuasion, remonstrance, or entreaty, but not for coercion or penalizing noncompliance. To justify compulsion, the conduct must be calculated to produce evil to someone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of social accountability — conduct concerning others
rubrics_metrics.description: The only part of the conduct of any one, for which he is amenable to society, is that which concerns others; in the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may legitimately make an individual answerable when his actions affect external relations and the interests of others; where conduct affects only the self (directly and primarily), independence should be absolute. Objections based on possible indirect effects (through him) are to be considered separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity/capacity exception
rubrics_metrics.description: This doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties (not children or those legally regarded as minors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who require being taken care of must be protected against their own actions; the law may fix an age of manhood or womanhood. Similarly, 'backward states of society' where people are not capable of improvement by free discussion may legitimately be governed by despotism if necessary for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimately compelled positive acts for others' benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many positive acts for the benefit of others which a person may rightfully be compelled to perform (e.g., give evidence in court, bear his fair share in common defence, perform acts like saving a life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When it is obviously a person's duty to do something for others, society may make him responsible for not doing it. These are instances where compulsion is permissible because the acts are necessary for the interests of the society whose protection the person enjoys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for inaction vs action (omission vs commission)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may cause evil to others not only by his actions but by his inaction; to make one answerable for doing evil is the rule; to make him answerable for not preventing evil is, comparatively speaking, the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding someone responsible for omission requires more cautious exercise of compulsion and is justified only in clear and grave cases. Reasons for not imposing such responsibility must be special expediencies (e.g., the agent likely acts better when left to discretion or control would produce greater evils).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere of individual liberty — inward domain of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate region of human liberty includes the inward domain of consciousness: liberty of conscience, liberty of thought and feeling; absolute freedom of opinion and sentiment on all subjects, practical or speculative, scientific, moral, or theological.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty of thought is foundational; the liberty to express and publish opinions is practically inseparable from it, given its importance for the formation and defense of thought itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of tastes, pursuits, and personal autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle requires liberty of tastes and pursuits; of framing the plan of our life to suit our own character; of doing as we like, subject to such consequences as may follow, without impediment from fellow-creatures so long as what we do does not harm them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals should be free to pursue personal ways of living even if others think it foolish or wrong, provided no harm to others ensues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of combination/association with consent
rubrics_metrics.description: From individual liberty follows the liberty, within the same limits, of combination among individuals; freedom to unite for any purpose not involving harm to others, with participants of full age, not forced or deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associational freedom is part of liberty but constrained by the harm principle and by requirements of age, consent, and absence of deception or coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to protect against tyranny of prevailing opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection is needed not only against the tyranny of the magistrate but also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; society tends to impose its ideas and practices as rules of conduct on dissenters and to fetter individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social coercion can be more formidable than political oppression because it penetrates into details of life and 'enslaves the soul.' Thus limits on society's moral coercion are as indispensable as protection against political despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject basing social rules on mere preference or custom
rubrics_metrics.description: People commonly accept rules because 'their feelings... are better than reasons' and take preference as sufficient justification; but an opinion not supported by reasons is only a personal preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom is often mistaken for first nature; policy and law should not rest on unexamined preferences or the illusion that majority feeling equates to moral justification. Reasons should be demanded rather than accepting mere liking as grounds for general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard against censorship — fallibility and the value of discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: We can never be sure that the opinion we are endeavouring to stifle is false; to refuse a hearing because one is sure it is false is to assume one's certainty is absolute — all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of human fallibility, opinions need to be open to criticism; free discussion enables correction of errors. Silencing opinions robs present and future generations: if true, they lose truth; if false, collision with truth clarifies understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold argument about suppression: possible truth and utility of error's exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: First: the opinion attempted to be suppressed may be true; second: even if false, its being aired produces clearer perception and livelier impression of truth through collision with error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two hypotheses together provide justification for maximal freedom of discussion — suppressing error either risks silencing truth or deprives truth of sharpening through contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that judgments be corrigible — keep means of correction available
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgment is valuable because errors are corrigible; reliance on judgment depends on the capacity to set it right by discussion and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy and societal practices should maintain open channels for criticism and contestation so that facts and arguments can be presented and interpreted; without keeping 'the lists open' we forfeit the only practical method of approaching truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-evils test for imposing responsibility/control
rubrics_metrics.description: There are good reasons for not holding someone responsible where the attempt to exercise control would produce other evils greater than those which it would prevent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether to enforce responsibility or impose control, consider whether control generates greater harms (practical expediency). If so, defer to individual conscience and discretion rather than compulsion.
